extracted.subtask_description: A concise set of determinants and professional qualities used to decide what is news and how to report it effectively; intended to guide journalists in selecting, prioritizing, and crafting news stories. Emphasizes both objective news determinants (timeliness, impact, prominence, etc.) and essential reporting practices (accuracy, attribution, verification, fairness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Current events priority. Online deadlines occur every minute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that are recent or breaking (e.g., assassinations) are given priority; timeliness drives placement and prominence. In digital contexts, timeliness is continuous — updates and immediate publication matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The greater the number of people affected or the magnitude of effect, the more newsworthy (example: deaths of 9 Charleston firefighters affected a whole community). Use impact to justify prominence and depth of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-known individuals and institutions make events newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prominent people or organizations (celebrities, public officials) elevate otherwise similar events (e.g., Michael Jackson's death drew national attention compared with a local musician). Consider name recognition when assessing audience interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The closer to home, the bigger the story." Local incidents command more attention from nearby audiences (example: BTK case dominated Wichita but got minimal attention elsewhere). Consider cultural or emotional proximity as well as physical distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Disputes — physical, ideological, legal — are inherently newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict provides drama and narrative tension (sports rivalries, court battles, policy fights). Highlight opposing sides and stakes to explain why the audience should care.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Unusual
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary or unexpected situations attract interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singular or bizarre events (sinkholes, unexpected rescues) stand out against routine news. Use vivid detail to convey the extraordinary nature without sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Dormant issues become newsworthy when new circumstances arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topics may gain attention when linked to current debates or developments (example: fingerprint scanning in schools becomes newsworthy amid privacy concerns). Connect background/context to the new trigger that makes the story timely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative reporting that exposes injustice or danger to vulnerable populations; public service journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories pursued out of public interest or duty — revealing wrongdoing, threats, negligence — deserve publication even if they lack glamour. Emphasize evidence and potential remedies; stress reporter responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure facts are correct before publication. Verification and careful fact-checking are central; errors undermine credibility and can cause harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write plainly so readers can grasp facts and significance quickly. Organize information logically and avoid unnecessary jargon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey essential information without needless words; prioritize what matters to the audience. Brevity supports readability and accommodates tight space or attention constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify where information comes from — named sources, official documents, or anonymous sources with justification. Proper attribution builds trust and allows readers to assess reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check information with independent sources, documents, or records. Treat unverified claims cautiously and disclose uncertainty when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and Balance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include relevant viewpoints and responses from affected parties; avoid bias by seeking comment and providing context. Balance does not require false equivalence — weigh credibility of sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human Interest
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that evoke empathy or curiosity engage readers; use human detail to illustrate broader issues while respecting subjects' dignity and privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five W's and H
rubrics_metrics.description: Who, What, When, Where, Why, How.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Five W's and H to ensure completeness and to structure the lead and story. They serve as a checklist for essential factual elements a news story should answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: News Judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Discerning which events merit coverage and which deserve prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply multiple determinants together — several factors often justify a story's importance. Judgment develops through experience; weigh audience interest, ethical considerations, and newsroom resources when deciding coverage and placement.
